# TDPdf v1.30.0.0

**Three defects reported from the field — a strikethrough that got erased, a strikethrough that crossed out too much, and a Line tool that looked like it had vanished — plus the first groundwork for real redaction and real text editing.**

## Fixed

### Editing replacement text erased a strikethrough next to it

On a punch list where each row reads `Gathering Area Windows (5) (4)` — the old count struck through, the new one typed beside it — going back to change the new count removed the strikethrough.

Replacement text is drawn with no width limit, so text longer than what it replaced overhangs its own box. Clicking those overhanging characters missed the check for "you're re-editing an existing change" and created a *second* change instead. The white backing behind that second change then covered the strikethrough, on screen and in the saved file.

Clicks now land on the text as it is actually drawn. Separately, white backings are now always painted underneath other markup rather than in whatever order annotations happened to be added, so a strikethrough applied *before* an edit survives too.

### Strikethrough crossed out unrelated lines

On a list with labels down the left and numbers down the right, TDPdf reads all the labels and then all the numbers. A short drag between two points a few pixels apart on screen could therefore span dozens of rows, and every one of them got struck through.

Markup is now limited to the lines the pointer actually crossed.

This is also the answer to why strikethrough seemed to need several attempts before it worked. There was no stale state to clear — the gesture simply had a very narrow target, with one failure mode either side of it and no feedback when it missed, so retrying eventually landed on it.

### The Line tool looked like it was missing from the Shape bar

It was always there. It was drawn with an icon that renders as an empty square, sitting two buttons away from the actual Rectangle tool, so it read as a duplicate rectangle rather than a line. All four shape buttons are now drawn as the shapes they create.

## Changed

**TDPdf now runs on .NET 10.** .NET 9 went out of support in May 2026, so this is about staying on a supported runtime rather than any new capability. Nothing changes about how you get or run TDPdf — it is still one self-contained `TDPdf.exe` with no runtime to install.

**The About box no longer carries the "Forked from SteveTheKiller/KillerPDF" line.** That credit now lives under Help > Third-Party Licenses, together with the formal statement that TDPdf is a modified version of that work, and it remains in `NOTICE` and `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`. Nothing has been taken away — TDPdf has simply diverged far enough that a one-line "forked from" stopped describing the relationship honestly in either direction.

**Help > Privacy Policy** now opens a proper hosted page instead of a file listing.

## Third-party licenses

**Help > Third-Party Licenses** is new, and a `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` is now attached to every release.

TDPdf ships as one self-contained executable, which means roughly 35 open-source components are physically inside the file you download — PDFium and the eleven libraries bundled within it, Leptonica, the Tesseract engine, PdfPig, PdfSharpCore, ImageSharp, OpenTelemetry, and the .NET runtime packages. Their licences require that their copyright notices and licence texts travel with the binary. Until now only one of them was credited, and only in a repository file that anyone downloading the `.exe` never saw.

The full notices are now embedded in the application, attached to each release, and included in the source bundle. Nothing changed about what TDPdf ships — only about what it tells you it ships. Every bundled licence is compatible with the GPLv3 that TDPdf itself is released under.

## Groundwork

Nothing user-facing here yet, but this is what redaction and true text editing are built on, and one piece of it changes what TDPdf writes into your files.

### OCR text is now written as properly invisible text

When TDPdf OCRs a scan it lays an invisible text layer over the image so the page becomes searchable. That layer used to be drawn in fully transparent ink. It is now written using the PDF format's own "invisible text" mode instead — and the transparent ink is kept as well, so it cannot become visible even if one of the two is ever stripped.

The change is that the layer is now *identifiable*, which it never was before. That matters because:

- **Redaction has to be able to find it.** A scanned page's invisible text survives any change to the picture, so redacting the image alone would leave the words behind. Transparent text is indistinguishable from ordinary text; text in invisible mode is not.
- **Editing a page can't accidentally reveal it.** The rendering engine preserves the invisible mode when it rebuilds a page.
- **Other tools stop mistaking it for real text.** OCRmyPDF explicitly documents that it cannot tell "technically printable" OCR text from genuine text and will refuse to redo it. Transparently-inked text falls straight into that trap.

Existing files are untouched; this applies to pages OCR'd from this version onward.

### A safety check before any page gets rewritten

Removing words from a page means rebuilding that page's contents, and rebuilding is lossy in ways the PDF engine never reports: non-RGB colour (CMYK, spot colours, ICC profiles), gradients, inline images and soft masks are all silently dropped. On a scanned page none of that is present. On a printed invoice or a chart, removing one word could recolour or delete something else entirely.

TDPdf now detects those pages up front, so redaction can fall back to a slower but safe method rather than quietly damaging the file — and tell you it did.

### TDPdf now checks what its PDF engine can actually do

Which editing operations are possible depends on the exact PDF engine bundled with the build. The current one cannot remove content nested inside form objects, which is precisely where scanned pages keep their text. Rather than assume, TDPdf now checks on the machine it is running on. A future engine update will enable the better path automatically instead of failing partway through a save.
